title: Reading the notebook through
hook: twelve books, never meant to be read by anyone else, now read in order

segments.voice: Yesterday: between two teachers, the freed slave and the rich courtier. Your line was two teachers. What would each have said about your day? Day five hundred twenty-one.

Picture finding someone's private journal. Not a memoir written for readers. The real thing: notes to self, repeated reminders, the same struggle written down again three months later because it hadn't gone away. Now picture that the writer was the most powerful man in the world, and that he wrote much of it in an army camp, at war. We've met Marcus Aurelius many times on this path, a line here, a passage there. Starting today, for about four months, we stop dipping in. Reading the notebook through.
screen: `SOMEONE'S PRIVATE JOURNAL.` → `THE EMPEROR, IN CAMP.` → `READING THE NOTEBOOK THROUGH.`

segments.voice: First, the writer. Marcus Aurelius was emperor of Rome from 161 to 180. He was trained in Stoic philosophy from his youth, and for years he jotted down notes to himself. He wrote them in Greek, the language of philosophy for educated Romans, not his native Latin. Second, the title. We call the book the Meditations, but that's not what he called it, as far as we know. The Greek manuscripts carry a heading that means something like to himself. Scholars think a later copyist may have added it. Either way, it's honest. These are things a man said to himself. Third, the shape. Twelve books, of uneven length. Inside them, short entries: some a single line, some a page. The section numbers we use are later editors' work, and editions sometimes divide them differently. It doesn't read like an argument. It reads like someone coming back, again and again, to the same few things he needs to remember. Fourth, it nearly vanished. For centuries the book is barely mentioned. The first printed edition, in 1559, was made from a manuscript that's since been lost. One more house fire, one more careless librarian, and we wouldn't have it. So here's the plan. Twelve books, in order, about ten days each, with a few days at the end to close the notebook. Book one is different from all the rest. It's a list of debts: what Marcus learned from each person in his life, one by one, starting with his grandfather. In order now.
screen: `AN EMPEROR'S NOTES, IN GREEK.` · `TITLED, PERHAPS LATER: TO HIMSELF.` · `TWELVE BOOKS OF SHORT ENTRIES.` · `IT NEARLY VANISHED.` · then, large: `IN ORDER NOW.`

segments.voice: If you have a copy of the Meditations, open it to book one, and just look at the first page. If you don't, picture it: a tired man by a lamp, a tent, a pen. Settle, and breathe. Then turn it around. If you kept a notebook to yourself, only for you, what's the one thing you'd need to write down most often? Let it come. The bell holds the time.
Reading the notebook through. Marcus Aurelius's twelve books of notes to himself, never meant for us, now read in order, from book one. Today's word.
Your line: in order now. Tonight, write one line to yourself, the way Marcus did: something you need to remember, in your own words. Day five hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Many readers of the Meditations read it slowly, an entry or two a day, and some keep their own notebook of reminders alongside it.

notes: Reign 161–180 (sole emperor from 169, with Lucius Verus 161–169); confirm the wording.
Title τὰ εἰς ἑαυτόν in the manuscripts, possibly not Marcus's own: confirm.
Editio princeps by Xylander (Zurich, 1559), from a now-lost Palatine manuscript; the other main witness is Vaticanus Graecus 1950. Confirm.
